mcqs.question: What's the recommended order of operations for this kind of live refactor?
options: Extract each branch into its own method first, classify what it varies on, then replace with the smallest pattern that fits
Introduce a full class hierarchy immediately, then extract methods afterward to fit inside it
Rewrite the entire function from scratch without running any existing tests
Ask the interviewer to skip the live-coding portion and describe the pattern verbally instead
mcqs.explanation: Extracting before classifying and replacing keeps every intermediate step compiling and testable, and lets you pick the right-sized pattern only once you know what's varying. Introducing a hierarchy first, skipping tests, or avoiding the live-coding exercise all undermine what the exercise is testing.

mcqs.question: Rewriting a type-branching if/else chain as `Map<String, ShippingCalculator>` with lambda values is an example of which pattern, implemented with less ceremony than a full class hierarchy?
mcqs.explanation: A lookup map of interchangeable behaviors, selected by a key and invoked uniformly, is Strategy — just implemented as lambdas in a map instead of one class per variant. There's no independent listener structure for Observer, no single shared instance for Singleton, and no shared algorithm skeleton with one varying step for Template Method.

mcqs.question: Branches in an if/else chain share about 80% of their logic and differ in only one step. Why might Strategy not be the best fit here?
options: Because Strategy can only be used when there are exactly two branches
Because extracting each branch into its own Strategy class would duplicate the 80% of logic that's actually identical across all of them
Because Strategy requires all branches to have zero shared logic by definition
Because lambdas cannot share logic with each other in Java
mcqs.explanation: When most of the logic is identical and only one step varies, giving each branch its own full Strategy class duplicates the shared 80% — Template Method, which factors the shared steps into one place and varies only the differing step, fits better. Strategy has no branch-count restriction, and the issue isn't a hard rule about zero shared logic — it's a practical duplication cost.

mcqs.question: An if/else chain has exactly two branches with no indication a third will ever be added. What's the strongest refactor recommendation?
options: Leave it as a conditional — introducing an interface and two Strategy classes here adds indirection for no real flexibility gained
Always convert it to a full Strategy hierarchy regardless of branch count, since patterns are inherently more maintainable
Convert it to a Singleton to guarantee only one shipping calculation happens at a time
Merge the two branches into one to eliminate branching entirely, regardless of correctness
mcqs.explanation: Two fixed branches with no growth signal don't justify the extra interface and classes a full Strategy hierarchy would add — that's cost without benefit. Blanket conversion 'because patterns are more maintainable' ignores this tradeoff, a Singleton addresses an unrelated concern, and merging branches without preserving correct behavior isn't a valid refactor at all.
